story_text.value:
Just received this:

We’re updating your privacy settings in Gemini Apps to give you even more control over your data and help make Gemini safer. We’ll start rolling out these changes in the coming weeks.

What’s changing: The Keep Activity setting currently controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models. Over the coming weeks, we will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. Using the first setting, you will be able to control how long your history is saved. Using the second setting,you will be able to separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models. With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training. If you turn off your History setting, future chats will be saved for around 2 monthsand used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.

How this affects your account: If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, your new settings will both be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on when this change is made, your new settings will both be on.

What’s not changing: You will still be able to change how long history is saved, choose an auto-delete period, and review or delete history manually at any time. As before, Google will not use your audio or Gemini Live recordings to improve Google services by default. You can change this at any time in settings.

title.value: Gemini is finally changing their privacy policy

story_text.value:
Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :)

What it does today:

- Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router.

- Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks.

- Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance.

We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results.

But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now.

We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions:

- 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency)

-The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps.

Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels.

So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8.

The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within

There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections.

You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results:

https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega...

Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback.

Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai.

We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

title.value: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium

story_text.value:
Over the last couple of years, I have observed many people (including myself) researching tricky topics by asking the same question to multiple AI's. If those answers conflict, we manually copy the answers back-and-forth between the AI apps to make them debate each other, to get a fuller picture of the topic.

I developed AI Spar to organize and automate this debate process. When the user asks a question:

1) Multiple AI's answer the question independent of each other.

2) An analyzer (also an AI model) finds the consensuses and disagreements between those answers, and what important points are missed by which answer.

3) For each disagreement point, each AI tries to defend its stance when presented with its original answer and the other side's opinion (it can concede if it feels the other side is right); and for each missed point, each AI tries to clarify whether it agrees with the point.

4) If all disagreement points have consensus, or the debate has reached max number of rounds, then go to 5); otherwise, go to 3) for the next round of debate with the latest arguments from each side.

5) The analyzer summarizes the debate, synthesizes a final answer, and lists the consensus points, resolved disagreements, unresolved disagreements, and clarified missed points.

Note that it might feel slow compared to those AI apps, because of all the steps taken above. Also worth a disclaimer: even if all AI's eventually agree on one point, that doesn't necessarily mean it's correct.

Some friends have been testing this system. They mention that sometimes reading the back-and-forth debate details is a lot more fun than reading the final synthesis.

Without signing in, you can try two separate questions, with entry-level models from 3 AI providers (Gemini, GPT, Claude).

Signing in enables additional features: asking follow-up questions, attaching images or PDFs, saving and sharing conversations. Also, stronger models from these providers are available for signed-in users. In addition, you can enable web-search grounded debates, and optional fact-checking during the debates. You pay as you go, no subscription at this point. Cost of each debate depends on the models and settings. We also support BYOK for these providers, with a separate system fee. CLI/API access is also available if you need them.

An interesting debate example: https://aispar.app/share/5f503127-4b4a-4c5c-9b2a-74081016b68... "Should junior developers use coding agents from their first day? " Even though all three AI's (Gemini, GPT, Claude) initially broadly agree on the surface, after the debate, each has made pretty big changes on the substance, and at the end there's still unresolved disagreement.

title.value: Show HN: AI Spar – Turn conflicting AI answers into a structured debate

story_text.value:
When Cursor got acquired a small question appeared in my head. Then after Conductor's acquisition by Meta it quickly became more itchy.

And then after a few months of asking myself "what if agentic coding tool wasn't built for exit?" I came up with Malini.

Those both were the best coding platforms (on the UI/UX front especially) I've ever used, so Malini aims to join what was best in both of them. Hope you might find it useful. Feel free to contribute or fork. * Cross-platform (Mac, Linux, Windows) is shortly down the road * AGPLv3 License

Features: * agentic merge-queue (thru gh cli) * variants picker (agent will show you many options for something you wanna build) * before/after turn summaries * frame-by-frame animations inspector * file/diff viewer * fully featured browser

It also has a bunch of pre-configured options to increase your token efficiency: * auto-compaction at 280k + re-attaching previous conversation summary (plus 16 percentage points of accuracy on the agentic eval i did on my few dozen chats) * built-in rtk; depending on a project up to 90% less tokens from bash calls

Looking for roast & feedback on how horrible is it!

story_text.value:
Hello, I’m Oscar. I’ve been leading dev teams from Barcelona with my cofounder Uri for a long time. We pushed the use of AI a lot, allowing an increase in the code shipment velocity, but our job as seniors moved from building to just reviewing. We also started to see a lot of drift in how devs were doing the code, less standards, less control, which caused more bugs and differences between what product department asked and what we shipped. It was impossible for us to keep reviewing everything by hand, so we decided to clone how we review as humans into a product: Revix AI.

In easy words, Revix main strength is that it extracts from your repo all the good practices and team standards, then on every pull request comments if anything moves from that. That, paired with PR status badges and targeted notifications allowed us to reduce review time by 54% on many teams, while increasing the confidence and reducing bugs on production.

We know there are other similar products around and they work fine, but we found that they trust too much on the LLM and focus just on bug hunting. Our philosophy goes further, we created a system that reviews the same as a senior engineer would do, not catching just bugs. We achieved to comment only on things devs actually fix and stop the noise.

Revix AI works on GitHub, Gitlab, Bitbucket and can sync with many other tools like Slack, Jira, Linear etc. Please feel free to request any other tool that we still do not support. We offer free reviews for any open source project, and for companies we do price per seat including a 14 days free trial.

hits.story_text:
Hello, I’m Oscar. I’ve been leading dev teams from Barcelona with my cofounder Uri for a long time. We pushed the use of AI a lot, allowing an increase in the code shipment velocity, but our job as seniors moved from building to just reviewing. We also started to see a lot of drift in how devs were doing the code, less standards, less control, which caused more bugs and differences between what product department asked and what we shipped. It was impossible for us to keep reviewing everything by hand, so we decided to clone how we review as humans into a product: Revix AI.

In easy words, Revix main strength is that it extracts from your repo all the good practices and team standards, then on every pull request comments if anything moves from that. That, paired with PR status badges and targeted notifications allowed us to reduce review time by 54% on many teams, while increasing the confidence and reducing bugs on production.

We know there are other similar products around and they work fine, but we found that they trust too much on the LLM and focus just on bug hunting. Our philosophy goes further, we created a system that reviews the same as a senior engineer would do, not catching just bugs. We achieved to comment only on things devs actually fix and stop the noise.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, since some time I have been experimenting with a new way to work with AI agents, instead of chatting with them in the usual sense, I wanted to work with them collaboratively (like people usually do in google docs or confluence). I think the chat based interface we use for these coding agents doesn't extend well to other use cases, like researching, thinking... or just having a general introspective session with AI.

I thought of having a simple markdown editor (like Notion), where you can just dump your thoughts (or documents) and then the AI agents can work off of them. I wanted to the app to be completely local so I don't depend on any cloud providers and can eventually run entirely offline with self-hosted LLMs in the future.

and that's basically Solipsist: https://solipsist.sh/

This is a completely new way to use and interact with AI agents, where your document is the main control surface. The AI agents can give back nicely formatted tables, images and other content. You can use this for planning, brainstorming, researching and more.

You can also create custom buttons which can trigger the same task again (like summarising new tickets assigned to you), these tasks can be run on some interval as well. Everything happens in the background daemon running on your machine, so you can just close the tabs/browser, and the Pi agents continue to run.

It is fairly extensible as well. Do give it a shot !

Github: https://github.com/pulkitsharma07/solipsist/tree/main

title.value: Show HN: Solipsist – Local Only Notes + Pi agents

story_text.value:
Yes that's a double negative because open source is not a business model. For years we've argued about value creation, sustainability and business models around open source and the fact that open source itself is inherently not a business model but as technology is evolving and AI has made the cost of producing code so cheap the question now stands, what is the value of open source, shared ownership and use and where do people create value. Hosting services still requires some level of infrastructure management so we are only going to trust so and so to do that. But in terms of software that we use. What then?

Somethings are easily replicated but I'd also say the hard fought lessons take time to relearn. AI is getting better at writing and iterating but then we're still subject to a lot of bugs and potential vulnerabilities.

If the cost is cheap, how do we value this software and the time involved to produce and maintain stable code. In some cases if it's for personal use maybe it doesn't matter but at the same time, we do need some stable foundations to start with.

As someone who failed to make money around open source (while still raising funding) I do wonder where the value is now derived on top of open source software and whether things like dual licensing will make a comeback.

title.value: Ask HN: What's the new open source business model

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I made LingDongNews, a small desktop news ticker.

With agents doing more of the work, we’re left with lots of little gaps in the day. They’re too short and scattered to do much else, so I made a small tool to check the news whenever there’s a moment.

English demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb6YXzWzQ-0

It stays on top as a single scrolling line. Click a story to expand it, then collapse it when you’re done.

You choose the sources: It supports RSS, Atom, JSON Feed, JSON endpoints and custom adapters.

You can highlight keywords you care about, or optionally connect your own AI API to highlight news matching your interests. Other news remain visible.

The interface is available in English and Chinese. The bundled sources are mainly Chinese financial news, but you can disable them and use your own feeds.

story_text.value:
Call Nara: someone to talk to, any time

Call Nara is a simple voice companion for older people, and for anyone who spends long days alone. You tap once and talk. There's no typing.

Nara greets you by name, asks how you are, chats and listens. Just ask by voice, and she can play music, hymns and movies, read from the Bible, and look through photos that you or your family have added, reading out the captions and chatting about them. If you nominate a family member, friend or carer, she can let them know if you seem upset or distressed.

Call Nara was designed with older people in mind, and with the families and friends who love them. It's built for everyone, so no one is left behind. Whatever your age, Nara is here for you.

Available now on iPhone and iPad (iOS only for now). Feel free to check it out
